chapters.title: Studio Management Scorecard
facts: Connecting commercial outcomes with the behaviours that drive them. September's results show a studio reaching more customers but generating fewer visits per person. Sales revenue stood at ₹15.29 lakh, while 259 classes produced 1,404 attendances and ₹13.06 lakh in recorded class revenue. Overall utilisation reached 42.6%. The contrast between customer growth and declining visit frequency is particularly significant. The number of attending members increased from 305 to 394 year-on-year, while average attendance per member fell from 4.84 to 3.56. The 78 customers who attended in both comparison months recorded 252 fewer visits this September. The studio received 189 September leads. Historical open-pipeline volume cannot be verified from the available frozen lead population. These findings point to three distinct management priorities: - Customer engagement: Rebuild visit frequency, particularly among established customers showing declining attendance. - Operational productivity: Improve the conversion of scheduled capacity into booked and attended places. - Commercial conversion: Improve lead progression, purchasing continuity and renewal ownership. The studio should assess these priorities together rather than treating sales, attendance and acquisition as independent performance measures.
chapters.subtitle: September's performance was constrained more by engagement and operating efficiency than by customer reach alone.

chapters.title: Sales & Revenue Health
facts: Higher spend per buyer helped offset a decline in purchasing customers. September closed at ₹15,29,410 across 196 distinct transactions (213 sale lines) from 139 unique buyers. Revenue declined by ₹35,322 (2.3%) compared with September 2025, while the number of buyers fell from 150 to 139. Average spend per buyer increased from ₹10,432 to ₹11,003, suggesting that higher individual purchasing helped cushion the reduction in customer volume. Memberships and Class Packages generated ₹12.77 lakh collectively, contributing approximately 83% of monthly sales revenue. The studio remains commercially dependent on converting customer interest into these two core product categories. The more important question is not simply how to increase monthly sales, but how to grow the number of purchasing customers while improving the consistency and quality of their subsequent purchases. Commercial implication: Protect the existing purchasing base, strengthen repeat-purchase opportunities and monitor whether customers are progressing towards longer-term commitments or relying increasingly on smaller, shorter-duration products.
chapters.subtitle: Revenue held relatively steady. The purchasing base became smaller.

chapters.title: Class Demand & Capacity Utilisation
facts: Only 43% of available class capacity translated into attendance. September delivered 259 classes, offering 3,293 available seats and recording 1,404 attendances. Overall utilisation reached 42.6%, compared with 41.8% in September 2025. This modest improvement should be viewed alongside the reduction in scheduled classes, from 273 to 259 year-on-year. The booking funnel reveals two separate opportunities. Of 1,604 recorded bookings, 1,404 resulted in attendance. There were 1,689 places without a recorded booking and 1,889 unoccupied places in total. Of the 200 bookings that did not convert into attendance, 199 were recorded as late cancellations; one booking was neither attended nor recorded as late-cancelled. This distinction is commercially important. Improving booking conversion and recovering cancellations can increase realised attendance, but neither replaces the need to address substantial unbooked capacity. Operational implication: The studio needs to manage three different outcomes independently: attracting bookings into available classes, improving attendance against confirmed bookings and ensuring the timetable reflects actual customer demand.
chapters.subtitle: The timetable has capacity. The challenge is filling it consistently.

chapters.title: Instructor Contribution & Effectiveness
facts: Assessing contribution beyond headline utilisation. Fourteen instructors collectively delivered 259 classes, generating 1,404 attendances and ₹13.06 lakh in recorded class revenue. Instructor-level utilisation ranged from 29.1% to 62.7%, demonstrating a substantial spread in attendance outcomes. However, these differences should not be interpreted as direct measures of teaching effectiveness. Individual results are influenced by the formats assigned, class frequency, timetable placement, available capacity and the customer groups attending each session. A meaningful assessment must therefore consider both absolute contribution and performance within comparable scheduling conditions. Management priority: Identify which instructors perform consistently well within specific formats and time slots, where additional support may improve results and where timetable allocation is affecting the fairness of existing performance comparisons.
chapters.subtitle: Instructor results vary significantly. The timetable must be part of the comparison.

chapters.title: Membership Health, Retention & Lapse
facts: Membership expiry is visible. Customer disengagement requires a separate attendance and purchasing assessment. The frozen September purchase cohort contains 325 membership records, including 121 paid purchases. Product status and usage reflect the uploaded export, rather than reconstructed September month-end outcomes. The median observed follow-up is eight days through month-end, not a completed membership lifetime. A product reaching its end date does not establish customer churn. Review subsequent purchases, latest attendance, entitlement validity and the interval since expiry before identifying customer inactivity. Distinguish members approaching expiry with healthy attendance, members with valid entitlements and declining engagement, and customers whose products ended without a subsequent recorded purchase. Each group requires a different response. Retention priority: Identify declining engagement while members still have valid reasons to return. The review’s broader historical counts and unused-credit totals cannot be verified from this frozen monthly cohort; retained historical reference tables must not be quoted as September findings.

chapters.title: Format Performance & Programming Strategy
facts: Evaluating reach, repeat attendance, utilisation and commercial contribution. Twelve formats collectively delivered 259 classes and ₹13.06 lakh in recorded class revenue during September. PowerCycle generated the highest attendance, with 410 visits, followed by Barre 57 (331) and FIT (277). Together, these three formats accounted for approximately 73% of monthly attendance. However, attendance volume alone does not establish which formats are performing most effectively. Each format serves a different commercial and customer purpose. Some attract a wider audience, some generate more regular attendance, and others support programme variety, introductory experiences or specialist demand. Format performance should therefore be assessed through four complementary measures: customer reach, repeat participation, utilisation and revenue per class. Special events and low-volume formats should be identified separately to prevent unusually high or low results from distorting decisions about recurring programming. Programming priority: Strengthen proven formats, improve weaker recurring slots and test opportunities for cross-format participation before making broad changes to the timetable.
chapters.subtitle: Not every format needs to play the same role in the business.

chapters.title: Revenue & Capacity Leakage

kpis.label: Value at average
kpis.detail: opportunity cost, not a booked loss

facts: Protecting booked attendance and maintaining pricing discipline. September recorded 199 late cancellations from 1,604 bookings, equivalent to a 12.4% late-cancellation rate. Using the studio's average delivered revenue of ₹931 per attendance, these cancelled bookings represent approximately ₹1.85 lakh in indicative attendance value. This figure should be interpreted as an opportunity estimate rather than confirmed lost cash revenue. Actual recovery depends on whether the cancelled seats could have been occupied by other customers and how those attendances would have been monetised. Separately, September's sales report records ₹1,45,209 in discounts. The two figures represent different challenges. Late cancellations reduce the conversion of booked capacity into realised attendance, while discounts affect the value captured from purchases. Both require clear operating rules, consistent measurement and individual accountability. Commercial priority: Improve attendance recovery from released seats while establishing greater visibility into discount approvals, product-level discounting and the revenue contribution of promotional activity.

chapters.title: Lead Funnel & Acquisition Health
facts: Trial progression is a useful intermediate acquisition milestone; subsequent purchasing and engagement remain the commercial outcomes. September’s frozen cohort contains 189 enquiries, 103 recorded trials and 12 recorded conversions at export. The recorded conversion rate is 6.3%. More recent enquiries have had less time to progress, so compare cohorts over a consistent observation window. The original historical lead export is unavailable. The review’s lifetime counts, open-pipeline totals and historical 26.1% versus 2.2% conversion comparison cannot be independently verified from the saved September population and are excluded from performance conclusions. Acquisition priority: Review trial scheduling, completion and follow-up ownership within the available cohort, qualify open opportunities and track trial-to-purchase progression without treating trial completion as the final acquisition goal.

chapters.title: Member Engagement & Attendance Behaviour
facts: Understanding the visiting habits behind September's attendance. 394 unique individuals generated 1,404 visits in September, averaging 3.56 visits per attending member. However, the average conceals two very different engagement patterns. 205 individuals—52% of the attending base—visited exactly once during the month. At the other end of the spectrum, the most frequent 10% of members generated approximately 42% of all attendance. This distribution highlights the importance of managing engagement at an individual level rather than relying exclusively on an overall frequency average. Member engagement priority: Create distinct retention strategies for occasional visitors, emerging regulars and highly engaged customers. Each group represents a different opportunity to improve frequency and sustain the studio's existing attendance base.
chapters.subtitle: Half the attending members visited only once. A small group generated nearly half the attendance.
